**Observation Log:**

- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/11 (Thu) 12:57
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The hierarchy of grammatical units includes: Sentence, Clause (Independent or Dependent), Subject, Predicate, Object, Complement, and Modifier.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The structure of a Sentence includes: 
  - Clause (Independent or Dependent)
    - Subject (if present)
      - Word (Noun, Pronoun, if present)
        - Letter
      - Phrase (Noun, if present)
    - Predicate
      - Verb Phrase (Main Verb, Auxiliary Verb, if present)
        - Word (Verb, if present)
          - Letter
        - Phrase (Verb, if present)
    - Object (if present)
      - Word (Noun, Pronoun, if present)
        - Letter
      - Phrase (Noun, if present)
    - Complement (if present)
      - Word (Noun, Pronoun, Adjective, if present)
        - Letter
      - Phrase (Adjective, if present)
    - Modifier (Adjective, Adverb, if present)
      - Word (Adjective, Adverb, if present)
        - Letter
      - Phrase (Adjective, Adverb, if present)
  - Phrase (Noun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Prepositional, Gerund, Infinitive, if present)
    - Word (Noun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, if present)
      - Letter
- [USER] Suggested to represent grammatical units as layers rather than a hierarchy, with sentences at the top, followed by clauses and phrases, then words, and finally letters at the bottom.
- [USER] Proposed a separate layer cake for subject, predicate, object, and complement, questioning how they could fit into the main layer cake.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The layer cake model includes:
  - Top level: Sentences
  - Next level: Clauses (Independent and Dependent) and Phrases
  - Next level: Phrases
  - Bottom level: Words
  - Bottom level: Letters
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Subject, predicate, object, and complement can be added as separate layers to the main layer cake, depending on context and language structure.
- [USER] Asked how words in English differ from words in Chinese in terms of construction.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Differences between English and Chinese words include:
  - Orthography: English uses the Roman alphabet; Chinese uses characters (Hanzi).
  - Word formation: English uses morphemes (prefixes, suffixes); Chinese words are often monosyllabic and can be compounds.
  - Word meaning: Chinese characters can have multiple meanings and functions; English words typically have one specific
